title: Habituate What You Can, Motivate What You Can’t
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart draws a practical distinction between motivation and habit as classroom-management tools: motivation enlists the will and is necessary for a class culture where students feel credibility, value, belonging, and success, but routines and procedures remove the need for will altogether once they're established. Using the start of class as his example, he argues that a class without a consistent opening routine will eventually wear down even the most motivated group and put unsustainable daily pressure on the teacher. He notes that routines only work if the teacher, not just the students, is perfectly consistent about running them -- and recommends James Clear's four-lever framework (make wanted behavior obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying; make unwanted behavior the reverse) for building that consistency. His conclusion is the title itself: habituate what you can, motivate what you can't, so that motivation is conserved for the harder work (debates, writing, text-based lessons) that habit can't cover.
points: Central distinction: motivation 'enlists the will' and requires ongoing effort, while a well-established routine 'harnesses the granite strength of habit' and requires almost none.

He identifies the start-of-class routine as a high-leverage example: without one, even a motivated, well-cultured class becomes 'antsy, distracted, jittery' and puts unsustainable daily pressure on the teacher to improvise.

A routine only works long-term if the teacher habituates their own follow-through first -- 'it really is a good idea to be perfectly consistent' in running it, even though perfectionism is otherwise unwarranted in teaching.
He imports James Clear's four-lever habit framework (obvious, attractive, easy, satisfying -- and their inverses for breaking bad habits) as the practical mechanism for building classroom routines.
quotes: But at the same time, wherever and whenever you can, you want to create the routines and procedures that make motivation unnecessary. Motivation, after all, is about enlisting the will. But routines and procedures? These harness the granite strength of habit.

BUT if those students don’t have anything that they’re used to doing at the start of class, even the most motivated and kind-hearted groups are going to struggle eventually. They’ll get antsy, distracted, jittery.
But here’s the most important thing about routines: since they depend so much on consistency, they’ve got to become habitual for you, too.
In nearly all areas of teaching, perfectionism is uncalled for. But when it comes to reinforcing habit, it really is a good idea to be perfectly consistent.
Thus for both us and for our students, the idea is straightforward: habituate what we can, then motivate what we can't. And throughout it all, simplicity wins the day.
The gist: We want motivation-rich environments all across a student’s school day. The five key beliefs methodology works great for that. But wherever you can, mess around with habit creation, too.
